transcript.speech: I posted a video asking which loading state you prefer:
a skeleton screen, a spinner, a progress bar, or no loader at all?
And what I learned from that video is there are two types of people in this world:
The ones that love skeleton screens,
And the ones who will go to war in the comments about their absolute hate for skeleton screens.
Here's why I think people hate them. Skeleton tends to show up
when your connection is bad.
So your brain links the visual with the negative experience.
We have been trained that these boxes mean slow connection.
Now, if one shows up even for just two seconds, you still attribute it to that.
And the research is actually split, but there's also not that much research on this.
One study tested skeletons against spinners and even blank screens.
And the skeleton felt the slowest of the three.
But a latest study found the opposite that skeleton screens can be perceived faster.
But only when done a specific way.
And that means that the skeleton did have to be animated,
no static gray boxes.
The animation had to have the shimmer wave, not the pulsing fade.
The wave had to move slow and steady, not fast.
And it had to sweep left to right.
If you get all of that right, skeletons might feel faster.
And speaking of doing it right, skeleton screens are a promise. It's promising a layout.
So if the real content loads in a different place than the boxes show, that everything jumps around, that's a broken promise, and it will trigger people.
But at the end of the day, skeleton screens are only meant to exist for a couple of seconds,
because they give you zero information about how long you're going to be waiting.
So your best use case is when you know your data arrives in less than three seconds.
But the catch on the engineer side of it, when the connection is bad and it takes longer to load,
actually detecting that and switching from a skeleton to a progress indicator is genuinely hard to build,
so most apps just don't do that.
So users just stay stuck staring at this way longer than they should.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Skeleton screens are perceived as faster only if they feature an active left-to-right shimmer wave animation moving at a slow, steady pace rather than static grey boxes or pulsing fades.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Mobile mockups demonstrating labeled animation variants (Animated, Static, Shimmer Wave, Pulsing Fade, Fast, Left to Right Sweep).
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Static skeleton screens, pulsing fades, or excessively fast animations can increase perceived wait time or frustrate users.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Animate skeleton screens using a slow, steady shimmer wave that sweeps from left to right.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Replace static gray placeholders or pulsing fades with a steady, left-to-right shimmer animation.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Perception research indicates that specific animation direction and steady movement reduce perceived loading times.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Skeleton screen design in mobile and web user interfaces.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Skeleton screens must accurately reflect the layout of the incoming content to avoid visual layout shifts when content loads.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Mobile phone screen graphic showing simple rectangular skeleton bars loading into a completely different blue card layout, causing visual jumpiness.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: When loaded content position does not match the skeleton placeholders, items jump around, causing visual discomfort and breaking user expectation.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Ensure skeleton placeholders mirror the exact structure, size, and layout of the real content.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Match visual dimensions and alignment of skeleton elements directly to incoming layout components.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Skeletons create an implicit visual promise of the layout; failing to match it creates visual clutter and frustrates users.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Layout skeleton design for feed and page components.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Skeleton screens should only be used for fast loads under three seconds; longer loads require switching to explicit progress indicators.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: UI mockup showing a skeleton loader transitioning to a spinner with text 'Just a moment...' after a delay.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Skeleton screens provide no status or time feedback, leaving users stuck staring at placeholders during poor network conditions.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Reserve skeleton screens for fast loads (<3 seconds) and programmatically switch to a spinner/progress bar if data fetching takes longer.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Detect slow connection timeouts and transition the visual loading state from skeleton cards to a progress indicator.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Skeletons convey zero information about wait time; prolonged skeleton display associates the visual pattern with bad connection quality.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Loading feedback design across web and mobile applications.
creator_derived_lessons.stated_exceptions: Engineering complexity in dynamically detecting slow loads and switching indicators.
